newsitem.title: FRANCE: French troops patrolling Bangui as precaution - Paris.
newsitem.headline: French troops patrolling Bangui as precaution - Paris.

text.p: France confirmed on Saturday that its troops were patrolling the Central African Republic capital Bangui after a fresh mutiny by dissident soldiers but played down the deployment as a routine precaution.
"There have been some incidents. We have taken the usual precautions in this type of situation," Foreign Ministry spokesman Jacques Rummelhardt contacted by Reuters said.
The spokesman insisted that foreigners in Bangui, including French nationals, were not in danger and said Paris was in close contact with the Central African authorities.
Earlier, a French government official said French soldiers had been deployed in Bangui "to assure the safety of certain sensitive areas".

The official was speaking after witnesses reported that French forces as well as members of the Central African Republic's presidential guard were guarding Bangui's deserted centre following the mutiny.
President Ange-Felix Patasse, in Rome for the World Food Summit, denied there had been a mutiny.
"Some common law prisoners have escaped and are trying to create panic," he said. "That is all."
France has a key military base in the country under defence accords between Paris and its former African colonies.

The Central Africa base has been key in France's long history of military intervention in Africa, including Rwanda and neighbouring Zaire, where Paris is again preparing to send troops in a multinational mission to help war refugees stranded by fighting between Zairean forces and Tutsi rebels.
Central African Republic troops have revolted twice already in recent months, last May and in September 1995.
On both occasions, the rebellion was quelled with help from the French military.
The French government official said the latest revolt was triggered when Central African security forces attempted to arrest a former mutineer.

Army soldiers then forcibly took weapons from the armoury and began moving from the eastern districts of the capital to the city centre where the presidential palace, the radio and television station and Patasse's residential villa are located.
"They broke into the armoury around midnight and stole arms and then firing broke out," a senior loyalist army officer told Reuters.

Another soldier in the main Kasai barracks outside the capital said by telephone that about 200 soldiers from the camp had gone to various parts of the city to try to disarm militiamen loyal to Patasse.
